parts.problem_md:
**Depth study C: Russia 1905–1941**

Discuss the importance of propaganda and culture to Stalin's control of the Soviet Union.
parts.solution_md:
Stalin's regime relied on far more than the secret police alone to secure the obedience of ordinary citizens across the whole of the Soviet Union.

The first facet, and perhaps the most visible one, is the cult of personality that Stalin's government built around him [R]. Portraits, photographs and statues presented Stalin as a god-like father figure and 'Uncle Joe', spread across the USSR, while Pravda remained the only legal newspaper and Western radio was banned [R]. Parades celebrating the October Revolution and May Day took place every single year in Red Square, with ordinary citizens carrying his image or performing before him [R]. This mattered because it gave ordinary Soviet citizens a constant, unavoidable reminder of Stalin's authority in almost every public space they entered, from the workplace to the classroom, a reminder that required no direct threat to enforce because it simply became part of everyday Soviet life [E].

The second facet, closely linked to the first, is the deliberate rewriting of Soviet history itself [R]. The government edited photographs to remove purged officials, such as Yezhov after his execution in 1940, and rewrote textbooks so that Stalin, rather than Trotsky, stood beside Lenin during the October Revolution [R]. This was significant because it did not simply celebrate Stalin's present authority; it manufactured an entirely false past in which his leadership had always looked inevitable and deserved, denying Trotsky, the man who had actually organised the seizure of power and led the Red Army to victory, any place in the story at all [E].

The third facet is Stalin's control over Soviet culture in the widest sense, reaching well beyond politics alone [R]. Churches were closed and priests arrested, leaving only around one in forty churches active by 1939, while Islamic mosques were banned [R]. Schools and youth groups such as the Young Pioneers taught loyalty to Stalin from childhood, and artists and writers were forced to follow Soviet Realism, a style requiring them to glorify workers and socialism, all monitored by the NKVD [R]. This reached areas of daily life that arrests alone could never fully control, shaping what people believed from early childhood rather than merely what they dared to say as adults, so that many young Soviet citizens grew up never having encountered an alternative version of events at all [E].

The fourth facet, and the most important qualification of all, is that none of this ever worked in true isolation from terror [R]. The same NKVD that monitored artists also ran the purges and staged the show trials, and citizens who might otherwise have doubted the propaganda knew exactly what happened to those who acted on their doubts [E]. Around 70% of the Central Committee of 1934 was eventually arrested and shot, and even Yagoda, the head of the NKVD who had helped enforce this system, was himself tried and executed in 1938 [R]. This gave every portrait of a benevolent 'father of the nation' a very different, far more sinister meaning underneath its surface [E].

These facets connect closely. Propaganda persuaded people what to think, and the fear of the NKVD stopped them acting differently even when they were not persuaded, so culture and terror functioned as two halves of a single, deliberately connected system of control rather than as genuine alternatives that Stalin could have relied on separately [A].

On balance, propaganda and culture were highly important instruments of Stalin's regime, but their importance depended entirely on the terror that ran alongside them rather than on anything they achieved standing independently on their own [A]. A cult of personality unsupported by real fear could have been mocked or ignored, but one reinforced by the knowledge of the purges and the GULAG became something citizens found genuinely dangerous to doubt aloud [A]. Culture shaped what Stalin's regime looked like from the outside, presenting a united, loving and grateful population; terror is what made that carefully constructed image genuinely impossible to challenge from within, since anyone tempted to question it had good reason to fear exactly what had happened to the Central Committee of 1934 [A].

parts.problem_md:
**Depth study C: Russia 1905–1941**

Discuss the reasons why Stalin launched the Purges.
parts.solution_md:
Stalin's rule as a whole is estimated to have caused the deaths of more than 20 million Soviet people, a toll even higher than the number killed under Hitler's regime in Germany, and the purges Stalin launched from the mid-1930s were a major contributor to this figure [R]. Historians disagree sharply about what actually drove such extreme and sustained violence against Stalin's own people.

The first facet is political paranoia rooted directly in the bitter power struggle that had brought him to power in the first place [R]. Stalin had won a bitter contest against Trotsky, Zinoviev, Kamenev and Bukharin, and by the mid-1930s he distrusted anyone with previous links to Lenin or Trotsky, believing many party members wanted to overthrow him [R]. He wanted total loyalty from Soviet citizens and used fear to secure it, believing that only the total elimination of anyone who might plausibly challenge him could guarantee his own survival in power, so eliminating potential rivals was central to his purpose from the very start of the purges [E].

The second facet is the specific, dramatic event of the assassination of Sergei Kirov in December 1934 [R]. Kirov was a senior Politburo member who wanted to reform Stalin's harsh economic policies, and many historians believe Stalin organised his murder by Leonid Nikolayev [R]. Whatever the truth, Stalin used the killing to claim an anti-Stalinist conspiracy had been uncovered, and this directly triggered the Moscow Trials against Kamenev, Zinoviev, Bukharin and Rykov [R]. The assassination gave Stalin both a public pretext and a genuine sense of urgency that turned private suspicion into mass arrests, show trials and executions on a scale the USSR had not seen since the Civil War itself [E].

The third facet is economic rather than purely political in character [R]. Stalin wanted the USSR to 'catch up' industrially with the West through rapid industrialisation, and the purges let him accuse anyone who missed production targets of sabotage, which frightened the wider workforce into working harder [E]. Arrested workers also became a source of free labour within the GULAG system, working under harsh conditions in the camps of Siberia to build roads, mines and canals the state needed, so the purges directly served Stalin's industrial ambitions as well as his political security [E].

The fourth facet is the sheer breadth of the many different groups targeted, which shows clearly that the purges served more than one single purpose at once [R]. Around 70% of the Central Committee of 1934 was arrested and shot, showing the political target was real, while around 350,000 minorities including 140,000 Polish people were tried, and kulaks made up roughly half of all arrests among peasants and workers [R]. Even the NKVD itself was purged from 1938, when Stalin had Yagoda and 23,000 officers executed because he believed the organisation knew too much about his own methods [R]. This range shows the purges were never aimed only at Stalin's old political rivals from the power struggle of the 1920s, but reached into every level of Soviet society, from the most senior general to the most ordinary peasant [E].

These facets are closely connected. Kirov's assassination provided the specific trigger, but it only led to purges on this scale because Stalin's underlying paranoia and his economic ambitions were both already present and actively looking for an opportunity to be acted upon; a single assassination could not by itself explain a terror that ultimately killed an estimated 20 million people over more than a decade [A].

On balance, political motives were the most important reason the purges happened in the first place, though economic motives clearly shaped how far and how deeply they were then allowed to spread across Soviet society [A]. Stalin's insecurity after the power struggle and his fear of anyone connected to Lenin or Trotsky explain why the purges began, targeting the old Bolsheviks first, but his desire to industrialise the USSR quickly explains why they grew to include managers, engineers, ordinary workers and eventually even the NKVD that carried them out [A]. Without the political fear generated by the power struggle, the purges would probably never have started at all; without the economic ambition to industrialise at speed, they might never have reached so deep into ordinary Soviet life, sweeping up managers, engineers and peasants who had never shown the slightest interest in politics [A].

parts.problem_md:
**Depth study C: Russia 1905–1941**

Discuss the reasons why Stalin, rather than Trotsky, became the leader of the USSR by 1929.
parts.solution_md:
By December 1929 Stalin had become the undisputed leader of the USSR, defeating far more prominent rivals including Trotsky, the hero of the October Revolution who had built and led the Red Army to victory in the Civil War [R]. This was a remarkable outcome, since Stalin had played almost no part in the events of October 1917 himself [A].

The first facet is Stalin's use of his position as General Secretary [R]. From 1922 the role gave him control over appointments throughout the party, letting him build a personal support base that even Lenin grew suspicious of [E]. This organisational power let Stalin place loyal officials in key positions throughout the party bureaucracy and out-manoeuvre rivals who had far greater personal reputations but no equivalent control over the party machine itself, since fame in 1917 counted for little against control of appointments in 1924 [E].

The second facet is Trotsky's own weaknesses [R]. Lenin's Testament had described Trotsky as capable but excessively self-assured and too preoccupied with administration, and this arrogance made him unpopular within the wider party even among those who respected his ability [E]. His policy of 'permanent revolution', demanding that the USSR spread communism worldwide, was unpopular compared to the right wing's 'Socialism in One Country' [R]. Prejudice against Trotsky's Jewish background, though he did not practise the religion, also turned some party members against him [R]. These weaknesses meant Trotsky could not build the alliances he needed even when the moment called for it, and his obvious talent as a soldier and orator only seemed to confirm to nervous colleagues that he could not be trusted with even greater power [E].

The third facet is Stalin's shrewd use of shifting alliances [R]. At Lenin's funeral he gave Trotsky the wrong date, ensuring he missed it while Stalin posed as chief mourner [R]. At the First Party Congress in 1924 he allied with Zinoviev and Kamenev against Trotsky, who was sacked from his post [R]. In 1926, once Trotsky was weakened, Stalin switched sides and allied with Bukharin to expel Trotsky and Zinoviev from the party in November 1927 [R], with Kamenev expelled from the Central Committee at the same time [R]. Finally, in 1928 and 1929, Stalin turned on Bukharin himself, who was removed from the Politburo in November 1929 [R]. This constantly shifting strategy meant Stalin never faced a united opposition at any point, defeating the left with the help of the right and then defeating the right in turn once the left no longer posed any real threat to him [E].

The fourth facet is the suppression of Lenin's Testament [R]. Lenin had explicitly warned that Stalin had concentrated unlimited authority in his hands and suggested he be removed as General Secretary, but a further stroke left Lenin unable to act on this himself [R]. In May 1924 the Central Committee considered the document, chose to keep it secret, and decided not to dismiss Stalin [R]. The one document that might have blocked Stalin's rise before it truly began, written by the one man whose authority nobody in the party could question, was buried by the very body that could have used it to remove him [E].

These facets connect closely. The Testament's suppression only mattered because Stalin already controlled enough of the party machine, through his position as General Secretary, to ensure it stayed hidden and had no consequences for him [A]. Trotsky's personal unpopularity, meanwhile, meant few in the Central Committee felt strongly enough about the Testament's warning to act on it even if they had wanted to remove Stalin instead [A].

On balance, Stalin's shifting alliance strategy was the most important reason for his victory [A]. His control of appointments as General Secretary gave him the tools to build support, and Trotsky's weaknesses gave him an opponent who could be isolated, but it was the specific, repeated tactic of allying with one wing of the party to destroy the other, then reversing the alliance to destroy what remained, that turned those advantages into total victory [A]. A less skilful operator with the same resources and the same rivals might well have failed to translate organisational power and Trotsky's personal unpopularity into the complete elimination of every genuine challenger by 1929, and could easily have been removed himself once his own allies realised what he intended for them next [A].

parts.problem_md:
**Depth study C: Russia 1905–1941**

Write an account of Stalin's use of culture and propaganda to control the Soviet Union.
parts.solution_md:
Stalin believed that controlling Soviet culture was essential to the survival of his regime, and he wanted all artists, writers and musicians across the Soviet Union to strengthen rather than challenge the state [D]. The Communist Party had used propaganda posters even under the Tsarist regime to win support, and Stalin expanded this heavily once in power [R]. Pravda became the only legal newspaper in the USSR, Western radio stations were banned, and the government heavily censored information and controlled public events so that the country always looked successful and united behind its leader [D].

Alongside censorship, Stalin relied on propaganda above all to build a cult of personality around himself [R]. Portraits, photographs and statues appeared across the USSR presenting him as a god-like figure, known affectionately as 'Uncle Joe' and the father of the Soviet people [D]. Parades celebrating the October Revolution and May Day took place every year, with participants carrying his image or performing before him in Red Square [D]. The government also rewrote history itself, editing photographs to remove Bolsheviks who had fallen from favour, such as Yezhov after his execution in 1940, so that surviving images showed only loyal, still-approved figures [D]. History textbooks were rewritten so that Stalin, rather than Trotsky, stood beside Lenin as the key figure of the October Revolution, erasing the man who had actually organised it and commanded the Red Army during the Civil War [D].

Control extended into religion, since communism viewed organised faith as a direct threat to state power [R]. Churches were closed and priests arrested, so that by 1939 only around one in forty churches remained active, and Islamic practices and mosques were banned across the Soviet Union too [R]. Education became another channel for control, as schools and youth groups such as the Young Pioneers promoted propaganda that glorified both Stalin personally and wider socialist values, ensuring loyalty to the regime was instilled from early childhood rather than left to develop naturally [D].

Music, literature and art were censored and closely monitored by the NKVD, and artists and writers were forced to follow Soviet Realism, a style of art that required them to praise workers and socialism rather than depict Soviet life honestly or critically [D]. Stalin recognised that culture could be far-reaching and powerful in changing the opinions of ordinary Soviet citizens, which is exactly why he insisted that every artist, writer and musician support rather than question the state's version of events. Together, these methods meant that almost every part of Soviet cultural and spiritual life, from the church to the classroom to the concert hall, was reshaped to serve and glorify Stalin's regime, leaving Soviet citizens with very few sources of information, belief or artistic expression that had not already been shaped by the state itself [D].

parts.problem_md:
**Depth study C: Russia 1905–1941**

Write an account of the Great Terror, 1936-1938.
parts.solution_md:
By 1934 Stalin had become increasingly paranoid, distrusting anyone in the party with previous links to Lenin or Trotsky, and determined that all Soviet citizens should show him total, unquestioning loyalty [D]. Sergei Kirov, a Politburo member who wanted to reform Stalin's harsh economic policies, was assassinated in December 1934 by Leonid Nikolayev, and many historians believe Stalin organised the killing himself [D]. Stalin used the assassination to claim that an anti-Stalinist conspiracy had been uncovered, and this triggered the Moscow Trials [R].

The Trial of 16 took place in 1936, accusing sixteen people, including Zinoviev and Kamenev, of disrupting the Five-Year Plans and murdering Kirov [R]. All sixteen were found guilty after torture and forced confessions, and all were executed [D]. The Trial of 17 followed in 1937, in which thirteen party officials were executed and four sent to the GULAG system [R]. The Trial of 21 came in 1938, accusing twenty-one people including Bukharin and Yagoda, the head of the NKVD, of the same crimes plus plotting to overthrow the government; all twenty-one were executed, and Bukharin used his trial to speak out about its corruption [D].

Beneath the NKVD's tactics lay mass arrests, torture used to force confessions, a growing network of informants and, from July 1937, formal quotas setting out how many arrests local officers had to make [D]. The terror reached far beyond the show trials themselves. Around 70% of the Central Committee members of 1934 were arrested and shot [R]. Around 350,000 minorities, including 140,000 Polish people, were put on trial, and four out of five regional Party secretaries lost their positions [R]. Eight senior generals and three out of five marshals were shot, leaving the armed forces having lost about half their officers by the end of Stalin's regime [D]. By 1938 Stalin turned against the NKVD itself, believing it knew too much, and had Yagoda and 23,000 of its officers executed, believing that the very organisation which had carried out his purges now knew far too much about his own methods [D].

Many historians consider the Great Terror to have ended in 1938, though others argue it did not truly end until Trotsky, sentenced to death in his absence by the Moscow Trials, was assassinated with an ice pick in Mexico in 1940 by the Spanish communist Ramon Mercader [D]. The Soviet government refused to take responsibility for his murder [R].

Purges continued even after the Great Terror officially ended, sending a further three million people to the GULAG system and killing around 750,000 more in the years that followed [R]. Managers, engineers and scientists were also swept up alongside the party, the military and ordinary workers, and a significant number of the educated intelligentsia who feared arrest chose to flee to the West rather than remain [D]. The consequences were severe: by the outbreak of the Second World War the Red Army had few experienced military leaders left, which contributed directly to the USSR's heavy early defeats during Operation Barbarossa in 1941 [D].

parts.problem_md:
**Depth study C: Russia 1905–1941**

Write an account of the power struggle to succeed Lenin, 1924-1929.
parts.solution_md:
Lenin's health had been failing since a stroke in May 1922 [R]. He had earlier survived an assassination attempt in 1918, when Fanya Kaplan shot him twice outside a Moscow factory, leaving a bullet lodged in his head that was slowly poisoning his brain [D]. A further stroke in March 1923 left him unable to speak, so he could no longer lead the Bolshevik Party actively, and he died on 21 January 1924 [R]. The Bolsheviks embalmed his body and built a mausoleum in his honour [D]. Between late 1922 and early 1923 he had dictated his Testament, criticising Trotsky as personally perhaps the most capable man in the Central Committee but excessively self-assured and too absorbed in administrative work [D]. Of Stalin, who had made his reputation as a Political Commissar during the Civil War and become General Secretary in 1922, Lenin warned that he had concentrated unlimited authority in his hands and was too rude, suggesting the party remove him and replace him with someone more tolerant and considerate [D]. In March 1923 Lenin had also learned that Stalin shouted at his wife on the telephone, which he regarded as unforgivable [R]. In May 1924 the Central Committee considered the document, chose to keep it secret and decided not to dismiss Stalin [R].

Lenin had not named a successor, and the party split into a left wing, made up of Trotsky, Zinoviev and Kamenev, who favoured 'permanent revolution', and a right wing, made up of Bukharin, Rykov and Tomsky, who favoured the more popular 'Socialism in One Country' [D].

Stalin moved first at Lenin's funeral, giving Trotsky the wrong date so that he missed it, while Stalin himself gave a speech and posed as chief mourner [D]. At the First Party Congress in 1924, Stalin allied with Zinoviev and Kamenev against Trotsky, using his position as General Secretary to build support within the party, and Trotsky was sacked from his post [R].

In 1926 Stalin switched sides, allying instead with Bukharin to remove Zinoviev and Kamenev, and promoting his own policy of 'Socialism in One Country' against their arguments [R]. In November 1927, Trotsky and Zinoviev were expelled from the Communist Party, and Kamenev was expelled from the Central Committee [R].

In August 1928, with the left now defeated, Bukharin tried to form an alliance with Trotsky against Stalin, but by then Trotsky had already been expelled from the party and the attempt came too late to matter [D]. Stalin turned against Bukharin and his allies who supported the New Economic Policy, and in November 1929 Bukharin was removed from the Politburo [R].

By December 1929, Stalin was the undisputed leader of the USSR [R]. parts.problem_md: How significant was Stalin's control of culture to his hold on power in the Soviet Union? Explain your answer.
parts.solution_md:
Stalin's regime attacked organised religion directly [R]. Churches were closed and priests arrested, so that by 1939 only around one in forty churches remained active, and Islamic mosques were banned too. This mattered because religion offered citizens a set of beliefs entirely outside Stalin's control, so removing it closed off a rival source of loyalty [E].

Control also reached deep into education and the arts [R]. Schools and youth groups such as the Young Pioneers promoted propaganda glorifying Stalin, while artists, writers and musicians were forced to follow Soviet Realism, a style praising workers and socialism, all monitored by the NKVD. This shaped what citizens believed from childhood onwards, not merely their outward behaviour [E].

This worked alongside an equally powerful cult of personality built on imagery [R]. Portraits, photographs and statues presented Stalin as a god-like father figure, parades such as those for the October Revolution and May Day displayed his image, and Pravda was the only legal newspaper while Western radio was banned. This made Stalin's rule feel natural and ever-present [E].

The regime also rewrote history itself [R]. Photographs were edited to remove purged officials, such as Yezhov, who was airbrushed out after his execution in 1940, and history books credited Stalin, not Trotsky, with standing beside Lenin in 1917. This made Stalin's rule appear permanent and inevitable, rather than something seized through an uncertain power struggle after 1924 [E].

However, control of culture worked best alongside fear rather than instead of it. Censorship and propaganda shaped what people said and did in public, but it was the NKVD's terror that actually stopped them acting on any private doubts they still held, so the two systems reinforced one another constantly [A].

On balance, Stalin's control of culture was highly significant, but chiefly as a support to terror and repression rather than as a genuine replacement for it [A]. Propaganda and censorship shaped how Soviet citizens understood their own society, but it was the fear of the NKVD and the purges that made open disagreement genuinely dangerous, so culture worked to reinforce a system of control that, underneath the parades and the portraits, ultimately rested on coercion and the fear of arrest [A].

parts.problem_md: 'Political motives were more important than economic motives in explaining why Stalin launched the Purges.' How far do you agree with this statement? Explain your answer.
parts.solution_md:
Political motives clearly drove the purges from the outset [R]. Stalin had become leader through a power struggle that left him with many enemies, and by the mid-1930s he had grown deeply paranoid, distrusting anyone with previous links to Lenin or Trotsky. This shows political control was central, since Stalin wanted a dictatorship with no opposition, so removing potential rivals secured the total loyalty he demanded [E].

A more specific trigger was the murder of Sergei Kirov [R]. Kirov, a Politburo member who wanted to soften Stalin's harsh policies, was assassinated in December 1934, and Stalin used the killing to claim an anti-Stalinist conspiracy existed, triggering the Moscow Trials against Kamenev, Zinoviev, Bukharin and Rykov. This mattered because it shows the purges targeted exactly the senior Bolsheviks who might realistically have challenged his leadership [E].

Economic motives were also genuinely significant, and one strand was Stalin's drive for rapid industrialisation [R]. Stalin wanted the USSR to 'catch up' with the West, so the purges let him accuse anyone who missed production targets of sabotage, frightening the wider workforce into working harder to avoid arrest. This mattered because it shows the fear the purges created was used deliberately to push industrial output forward [E].

A second economic strand was the free labour the purges generated [R]. Workers and other victims arrested during the purges became prisoners in the GULAG system, where they carried out forced physical labour, often under harsh Siberian conditions. This mattered because it shows the purges were not purely about Stalin's personal survival; the huge scale of arrests also gave the state a direct economic resource [E].

The two motives worked together rather than operating separately from one another [R]. Political victims, once arrested on political grounds, automatically became economic assets through forced labour in the camps, so the very same arrest could serve both of Stalin's aims at once [A].

On balance, this is true to a large extent: political motives were clearly the more important of the two [A]. The purges began with Kirov's assassination and the elimination of Stalin's political rivals, and the economic use of the victims' labour followed from arrests that had already been decided on political grounds. Securing his own power, not raising industrial output, was the underlying reason the purges began in the mid-1930s and why they began exactly when and how they did [A].

parts.problem_md: Which was more important in explaining Stalin's victory in the power struggle after 1924: his position as General Secretary or the divisions among his rivals? Explain your answer.
parts.solution_md:
Stalin's position as General Secretary gave him enormous practical power over the party [R]. From 1922 the role let him control appointments, so he could place loyal supporters throughout the party machine and build a personal support base, a build-up that made Lenin himself grow suspicious of Stalin before his death. This mattered because it gave Stalin a genuine organisational advantage over rivals such as Trotsky, who held no equivalent power to shape who filled positions across the party [E].

This organisational power was then used directly to win the leadership contest [R]. At the First Party Congress in 1924 Stalin used his position to ally with Zinoviev and Kamenev against Trotsky, and by 1927 that same control over appointments let him expel Trotsky and Zinoviev from the party altogether, with Kamenev expelled from the Central Committee at the same time. This mattered because, without the General Secretary's power over appointments, Stalin could not have manoeuvred so effectively against men who were far more famous than himself in 1924 [E].

His rivals' divisions were equally important [R]. The left, led by Trotsky, believed in 'permanent revolution', while the right, led by Bukharin, favoured the more popular 'Socialism in One Country', so the two sides could never fully agree on the future direction of the party. Trotsky was also widely seen as arrogant, and prejudice against his Jewish background cost him further support within the party. This mattered because it meant Stalin's most talented rival lacked the broad, united backing needed to challenge him directly [E].

Because the left and right could never agree, Stalin was able to exploit this directly [R]. He allied first with Zinoviev and Kamenev on the left to isolate Trotsky in 1924, then turned to the right to expel them in 1927, before finally turning on Bukharin and removing him from the Politburo by 1929. This mattered because a genuinely united opposition might have removed Stalin using Lenin's own Testament, which had explicitly called for exactly that outcome back in 1923 [E].

The two factors reinforced each other closely [R]. Stalin's control of appointments only worked because his rivals were too divided to see the pattern and unite against him before it was too late [A].

On balance, the divisions among his rivals were more important [A]. Stalin's position as General Secretary gave him the tools to exploit those divisions, but the tools alone would have achieved little against a genuinely united opposition. It was the left-right split, and Trotsky's personal unpopularity within it, that gave Stalin an opposition he could pick apart one piece at a time, turning an administrative post held since 1922 into undisputed leadership of the entire Soviet Union by December 1929 [A].

parts.problem_md: Discuss the importance of the NKVD to Stalin's control of the Soviet Union.
parts.solution_md:
**The first facet is that the NKVD operated without the restraints of law.** Formed in 1934 out of the earlier Cheka and OGPU, and combining the military and general police into one organisation, it was tasked with eliminating political enemies and needed neither evidence nor witnesses to make an arrest. From 1935 it could prosecute children as young as 12 as adults. The importance of this is that no Soviet citizen could establish their own safety. Innocence was no protection, because guilt was not what determined arrest, and a population that cannot predict what will get it arrested has no reliable way of staying safe except total compliance [E].

**The second facet is the scale that quotas made possible.** From July 1937 the NKVD worked to quotas for the number of arrests to be made. This turned repression into an administrative target rather than a response to actual opposition, and it meant local officers had to find enemies whether or not any existed. Terror on this scale could not have been generated by an organisation that waited for crimes to occur [E].

**The third facet is that the NKVD made fear self-sustaining through informants.** It built a network of informers and used torture to extract confessions. The effect was to push surveillance down into ordinary life, so that neighbours, colleagues and even family members might report a careless remark. This mattered more than the number of officers the NKVD employed, because it meant people policed their own speech continuously without any officer being present [E].

**The fourth facet is that the NKVD supplied the regime's other instruments.** The secret police administered the GULAG, the system of forced labour camps created in 1919 and largely located in Siberia, which held political opponents, kulaks, NEPmen, workers accused of sabotage, members of the military and artists who breached censorship. Conditions were lethal: overcrowded wooden lodges, little sanitation, no heating in the Siberian cold, and food rationed according to whether unattainable production targets were met, so that prisoners died of overwork, disease and starvation. The NKVD also produced the confessions on which the show trials depended, including the trials of 1936, 1937 and 1938 that destroyed Zinoviev, Kamenev and Bukharin. Without the NKVD neither the camps nor the trials could have functioned [E].

**The fifth facet is that terror alone did not hold the country together.** Alongside the NKVD ran an enormous apparatus of persuasion: Pravda was the only legal newspaper, Western radio was banned, and Stalin was presented in portraits, photographs and statues as a god-like figure and the father of the Soviet people. History was rewritten and photographs doctored to remove those who had been executed. Some Soviet citizens genuinely believed in the regime and its achievements. Control therefore rested on consent as well as coercion, and the NKVD explains only one half of it [E].

**Judgement.** The NKVD was the single most important instrument of Stalin's control, because it was the one on which the others depended [A]. Propaganda could be ignored privately in a way that arrest could not, and the cult of personality drew much of its force from the knowledge of what happened to those who questioned it. The camps and the show trials were both NKVD products.

But its importance is best stated more precisely than simply calling it the most important [A]. What the NKVD guaranteed was obedience, not belief. It could make opposition impossibly dangerous; it could not make the regime popular. Stalin's control was therefore built on two things working together, with the NKVD supplying the certainty of punishment and the propaganda machine supplying a reason to accept it. Of the two, the NKVD was the indispensable one, since a regime can survive without being loved but not without being obeyed [A].

parts.problem_md: Write an account of Lenin's Testament.
parts.solution_md:
Lenin's health had been failing since 1921. He had survived an assassination attempt in 1918, when Fanya Kaplan shot him twice outside a Moscow factory and left a bullet lodged in his head, and he suffered a massive stroke in May 1922. It was in this condition, between late 1922 and early 1923, that he dictated what became known as his Testament, setting out his views on the party's future after his death [R].

The document assessed the leading Bolsheviks in turn. Of Trotsky, Lenin wrote that he was personally perhaps the most capable man in the Central Committee, but that he had shown excessive self-assurance and was too preoccupied with the administrative side of the work. In other words Lenin thought him gifted but arrogant, and too absorbed in paperwork to lead. That judgement reflected Trotsky's record: he had proved himself in the October Revolution and the Civil War and was a gifted speaker and writer, but many in the party found him overbearing, and antisemitic attitudes among some members also told against him [R].

Lenin's remarks on Stalin were far harsher. He observed that Stalin, having become General Secretary, had concentrated unlimited authority in his hands, and that he was not certain Stalin would always use it with sufficient caution. He went further, writing that Stalin was too rude and suggesting that comrades find a way of removing him from the post and replacing him with someone more tolerant, more loyal and more considerate [R].

These views had specific origins. Stalin had risen quickly despite playing little part in the October Revolution, becoming Commissar for Nationalities in November 1917, making his reputation as a Political Commissar during the Civil War, and being appointed General Secretary in 1921. Lenin had grown suspicious as Stalin built a base of support personally loyal to him, and regarded him as cruel and uneducated, holding prejudiced views about his Georgian background. Matters came to a head in March 1923, when Lenin learned that Stalin had shouted at his wife over the telephone, which he regarded as unforgivable [R].

The Testament never had the effect Lenin intended. A further stroke in March 1923 left him unable to speak and therefore unable to remove Stalin himself, and he died on 21 January 1924. In May 1924 the Central Committee considered the document, chose to keep it secret and decided not to dismiss Stalin [R].

Its significance lies in that decision. The one man who might have blocked Stalin's rise had recorded his objection in writing, and the party leadership chose to bury it, leaving Stalin in the post from which he went on to win the struggle for power by 1929 [R].

**[15 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> To help identify where credit will be awarded, the following code has been used:
> 
> - Recall - [R]
> 
> Accuracy, coverage and sequence earn the marks, not explanation.
> 
> **Mark allocation**
> 
> - **11-15 marks:** the account includes the main events and developments and directly addresses the question. It is consistently supported by accurate historical knowledge and is logically sequenced.
> - **6-10 marks:** the account describes some events and developments relevant to the question. It is mostly supported by accurate historical knowledge and is structured in its approach.
> - **1-5 marks:** limited relevance to the question. Some accurate historical knowledge. Points are generally unconnected.
> - **0 marks:** no creditable material.
> 
> **Common errors**
> 
> Common errors which prevent an answer from achieving 11-15 marks include:
> 
> - Narrating the whole power struggle of 1924 to 1929. Stalin's manoeuvring against Zinoviev, Kamenev and Bukharin is a different question; this one is about the document.
> - Covering only what Lenin said about Stalin. The Testament assessed Trotsky too, and its criticism of both men is part of why it was so awkward for the party.
> - Omitting the suppression. The decision of May 1924 is the single most important fact about the Testament, because it explains why the document changed nothing.
> - Claiming Lenin named a successor. He did not, and saying so is a straightforward factual error.
> 
> **Alternative content**
> 
> - Lenin also created the USSR in December 1922, formally uniting Russia, Belarus, Ukraine, Georgia, Azerbaijan and Armenia, so the Testament was dictated at the same time as he was reshaping the state.
> - The Bolsheviks embalmed Lenin's body and built a mausoleum, which shows how far his authority was being turned into a cult even as his written wishes were being ignored.
> - Stalin deliberately misled Trotsky about the date of Lenin's funeral and then acted as chief mourner, which is a useful illustration of how he handled Lenin's legacy.
> - The criticism of both leading candidates made the document dangerous for everyone, which helps explain why the Central Committee preferred to suppress it.

> **[exam-tip]**
> - You do not need to memorise the exact quotations. Examiners expect you to know what Lenin thought of Trotsky and Stalin and why, so the substance matters more than the wording.
> - Organise by person: Lenin's condition, then Trotsky, then Stalin, then what happened to the document. That sequence is easy to follow and covers everything.
> - The March 1923 telephone incident is the detail most candidates miss and shows precise knowledge.
> - Always finish with May 1924. An account that stops at what Lenin wrote has left out the reason the Testament mattered.

parts.problem_md:
Stalin used many different methods to hold on to power.

Why did Stalin's government rewrite the history of the Russian Revolution?
parts.solution_md:
One reason was to destroy Trotsky's claim to be Lenin's rightful heir [R]. Trotsky had organised the October Revolution and commanded the Red Army, so anyone who remembered 1917 accurately could see that he, not Stalin, had stood closest to Lenin at the decisive moment. History textbooks were therefore rewritten to present Lenin and Stalin as the two key figures of the Revolution, with Trotsky pushed out of the story. This mattered because it turned Stalin's leadership from something he had manoeuvred his way into against rivals into something that looked natural and deserved, while Trotsky, by then in exile, could be presented as a traitor rather than as a man with a better claim [E].

A second reason was to make opposition feel pointless [R]. As officials were purged they were removed from the photographic record as well as from their posts, and Yezhov, once head of the NKVD, was edited out of published photographs after his execution in 1940. The message to anyone watching was that Stalin's enemies did not simply lose an argument or even their lives; they were erased, as though they had never held office at all. Combined with the cult that presented Stalin as the god-like father of the Soviet Union, this made opposing him feel not just dangerous but futile, and it discouraged people from associating with any figure who might later fall [E].

**[6 marks]**

> To help identify where credit will be awarded, the following codes have been used:
> 
> - Recall - [R]
> - Explanation - [E]
> 
> **Mark allocation**
> 
> - 6 marks are awarded for explaining two reasons.
> - Explaining one reason is worth 4 marks, rising to 5 marks where the explanation is supported by specific contextual knowledge.
> - Identifying or describing valid reasons without explaining them is worth 2-3 marks, with one mark for each identification.
> - Writing about the topic without addressing the question is worth 1 mark.
> 
> **Common errors**
> 
> Common errors which prevent an answer from achieving 6 marks include:
> 
> - Describing how history was rewritten rather than why. Doctored photographs and edited textbooks are the method; the marks come from the purpose behind them.
> - Writing a general answer about propaganda. Statues, parades and posters are worth a passing mention, but the question is specifically about rewriting the past.
> - Treating this as a question about censorship of the press. Banning western radio and running Pravda as the only legal newspaper controlled current information, which is a different aim from altering the historical record.
> 
> **Alternative content**
> 
> - Controlling the story of 1917 also protected the legitimacy of the Communist Party itself, since the Revolution was the founding event on which its right to rule rested.
> - The rewriting fed directly into the cult of personality, because a Stalin who had stood beside Lenin in 1917 was far easier to present as the father of the nation.
> - Because Pravda was the only legal newspaper and western radio was banned, most Soviet citizens had no way of checking the official version against any other account.

> **[exam-tip]**
> - Two explained reasons is the target. Each paragraph should end with what the rewriting achieved for Stalin.
> - Keep asking yourself 'so what?' after each piece of evidence. Saying Trotsky was removed from the textbooks is a description; saying it made Stalin's rule look legitimate is an explanation.
> - Naming Trotsky and Yezhov gives you the specific contextual knowledge that lifts a Level 3 answer from 4 marks to 5.

parts.problem_md:
Stalin used many different methods to hold on to power.

What happened in the Soviet show trials of 1936 to 1938?
parts.solution_md:
Leading Bolsheviks were put on public trial accused of crimes such as disrupting the Five-Year Plans, murdering Kirov and plotting to overthrow the government [1]. The accused confessed, having been tortured by the NKVD beforehand, and the judge already knew the sentence before the trial began [1]. In the Trial of 16 in 1936, sixteen people including Zinoviev and Kamenev were found guilty and executed [1]. The Trial of 21 in 1938 included Bukharin and Yagoda, the head of the NKVD, and all twenty-one were executed [1].

> **[mark-scheme]**
> To help identify where credit will be awarded, the following code has been used:
> 
> - 1 mark for each relevant point - [1]
> 
> **Mark allocation**
> 
> - 1 mark for each relevant point, up to a maximum of 4.
> - Four separate points are needed for four marks. Developing a point you have already made does not earn a second mark.
> - Accept all valid responses.
> 
> **Common errors**
> 
> Common errors which prevent an answer from achieving 4 marks include:
> 
> - Explaining why Stalin held the trials, or how effective they were. Both are worth marks on other questions, but this one asks what happened.
> - Writing about the purges in general. The gulags and the mass arrests are a wider topic; the question is about the trials themselves.
> - Saying only that people were 'put on trial and killed'. Naming who, when, or what they were accused of is what turns a vague statement into a creditable point.
> 
> **Alternative content**
> 
> - The Trial of 17 in 1937 tried party officials, of whom thirteen were executed and four sent to the labour camps.
> - Bukharin used his trial in 1938 to speak out about how corrupt the proceedings were.
> - The trials were staged and public, with the outcome decided in advance, which is what the term 'show trial' means.

> **[exam-tip]**
> - Keep each point in its own sentence so the examiner can count them.
> - Naming names earns marks. Zinoviev, Kamenev, Bukharin and Yagoda are all worth knowing, and naming a trial with its date counts as a point in its own right.
> - Four points is the whole task. There are no marks here for explaining Stalin's motives.

parts.problem_md:
Stalin used many different methods to hold on to power.

How complete was Stalin's control of the Soviet Union by 1941? Explain your answer.
parts.solution_md:
In politics his control was as close to total as a ruler can get [R]. The purges had torn through the Communist Party and the officer corps, so those who remained in post owed their survival to Stalin and had every reason to stay loyal. Behind them stood the NKVD, which needed neither evidence nor witnesses to make an arrest and which from 1935 could prosecute children as young as twelve as adults, and behind the NKVD stood the labour camps. Organised political opposition simply could not form under those conditions, because anyone who began to build it disappeared [E].

Control over what people were allowed to think was almost as tight [R]. Pravda was the only legal newspaper, western radio was banned, and the arts were censored and monitored. On top of this sat the cult of personality, with portraits, photographs and statues presenting Stalin as a god-like father of the nation, so that opposing him felt not merely dangerous but wrong. The regime even edited photographs to remove purged figures and rewrote the textbooks so that Stalin, not Trotsky, stood beside Lenin in 1917 [E].

Against this, control of the economy and of daily behaviour was much weaker than the propaganda suggested [R]. Workers and peasants moved around the country constantly and the government struggled to keep track of them. Many failed to meet their production targets and simply bribed officials to cover it up, or turned out substandard goods so the figures would look right. That is not a population doing what it is told; it is a population working around instructions it cannot meet [E].

There is also the problem of reach [R]. Stalin directly governed only central Russia and depended on party officials to run everywhere else, which meant his authority passed through exactly the kind of local officials who had an interest in reporting good news. The purges made this worse rather than better, because they stripped out skilled people from every sector and left the country short of the experts it needed [E]. Underground opposition groups, particularly among the young, also went on existing [R].

I partially agree that Stalin's control was complete [A]. Where control rested on terror it really was total, and by 1941 no one in the Soviet Union could organise against him and expect to live. But where control depended on people cooperating rather than fearing, it leaked badly, and the bribery, the shoddy output and the reliance on unsupervised local officials all show it. Stalin could make the Soviet people obey him; he could not make them work well for him, and the difference between those two things is what stops his control being complete [A].

**[10 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> To help identify where credit will be awarded, the following codes have been used:
> 
> - Recall - [R]
> - Explanation - [E]
> - Analysis - [A]
> 
> **Mark allocation**
> 
> - 10 marks require you to explain both sides and then support a valid judgement on 'how far'.
> - Explaining both sides without a supported judgement is worth 7-9 marks. Seven marks are given for one explanation on each side, with one further mark for each additional explanation on either side.
> - Explaining only one side is worth 4-6 marks, with one mark for each explanation.
> - Identifying or describing valid points without explaining them is worth 2-3 marks.
> - Writing about the topic without addressing the question is worth 1 mark.
> 
> **Common errors**
> 
> Common errors which prevent an answer from achieving 10 marks include:
> 
> - Describing the purges, the NKVD and the cult of personality one after another without ever asking how complete the resulting control was. Methods are evidence; the question is about the result.
> - Arguing only that control was total. An answer that never considers the limits is capped at 6 marks however detailed it is.
> - Drifting past 1941 into the Second World War. The date in the question sets the boundary.
> 
> **Alternative content**
> 
> - Collectivisation and the Five-Year Plans gave the state direct control over where peasants and workers lived and what they produced, which extended Stalin's reach into the countryside.
> - The scale of the machinery is itself evidence: the GULAG population passed two million by 1938.
> - A useful distinction is between public and private life. Open opposition was almost impossible, but what people did and said among themselves was far harder for the regime to reach.

> **[exam-tip]**
> - Aim for at least three explanations, two on one side and one on the other, then judge.
> - The strongest structure here is to separate the areas of life. Control over politics, over information, over the economy and over private behaviour were not equally complete, and saying so is exactly the kind of analysis Level 5 rewards.
> - Use 'fully' or 'partially' in your conclusion. A qualified judgement scores better than a flat yes or no.
> - Avoid listing methods. Every method you name should be followed by what it did or failed to do to Stalin's grip on the country.
